title: What if you could see heat, like a snake?

narration.heading: Heat vision
narration.text: You wake up, and everything warm around you is glowing, even in the dark.

narration.heading: Your heat
narration.text: Your body gives off heat as infrared light, mostly around ten micrometres. Your eyes can't see it.

narration.heading: The pit
narration.text: But some snakes can. Pit vipers, like rattlesnakes, have a heat-sensing pit between each eye and nostril.

narration.heading: Three times
narration.text: Heat sensing evolved three separate times in snakes: in pit vipers, pythons and boas.

narration.heading: How it works
narration.text: Here's how. Infrared warms a thin membrane, heat-sensing proteins fire, and the brain builds a picture.

narration.heading: Two pictures
narration.text: That heat map overlaps with what their eyes see. Heat and light, together.

narration.heading: In the dark
narration.text: In total darkness, they can spot something warm from several metres away, and strike.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? Those nerves can sense a temperature change of less than a thousandth of a degree.

narration.heading: Your call
narration.text: With snake senses, nobody could hide from you at night. Would you want heat vision?

titles: What if you could see heat, like a snake?
Some snakes can see your body heat in the dark
youtube.description: How pit vipers, pythons and boas sense the infrared heat your body gives off, combine it with what their eyes see, and strike in total darkness.

sources.claim: At body temperature, humans radiate mainly at wavelengths around 10 μm; infrared is invisible to people
Pit vipers, including rattlesnakes, have a heat-sensing pit between the eye and the nostril on each side of the head

Infrared sensing evolved independently in boas, pythons and pit vipers; a warmed membrane and the TRPA1 channel detect the heat; visual and infrared maps overlap in the optic tectum; pit vipers detect warm objects from several metres away in darkness; nerve sensitivity is estimated at under 0.001 °C
